newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: FEATURE - Developers bide time on Cambodian coast.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Developers bide time on Cambodian coast.

text.p: The pristine beaches of this sleepy port city in southern Cambodia roll straight out of idyllic travel brochures.
But despite several high-profile announcements of ambitious development projects, the coastline remains mostly untouched.
"We have the sea breeze, the white sand, the clear water and the fresh air. We have waterfalls. But we don't have development," said Sihanoukville Director of Tourism Teng Huy.
"No one has started working. We just have company names but no action," he said in an interview with Reuters.
Sihanoukville, one of Cambodia's most beautiful places, remains a quaint village -- good news for tourists who want a remote getaway but bad news for a government desparate for foreign money.
This is becoming increasingly familiar in the war-ravaged nation, analysts said.

Investors, concerned about political instability and the outcome of local and national elections expected in 1997 and 1998, were willing to gamble on land values but were cautious about implementing projects, they said.
The elections would not only be a roll of the dice for the candidates -- including co-Premiers Prince Norodom Ranariddh and Hun Sen -- but also a gamble for developers, analysts said.

Teng Huy said land speculation was the main force slowing development projects, noting that seafront properties have rocketed to $70 per square metre from about $6 two years ago. He said the skeleton of the high-rise Independence Hotel, abandoned in 1970s, remained the inelegant home of hundreds of squatters despite a contract with Malaysia's YTL Sdn Bhd for renovation.

King Norodom Sihanouk's former vacation home is a forgotten foundation barely protruding from quiet dunes, with no sign of the Ariston Sdn Bhd golf course -- expected to accompany a $1.3- billion resort and an international airport -- that would take its place.
And the future home of Club Med, a joint venture with Cambodia's Sokimex and Jakarta Holdings, is now decaying bungalows frequented only by the most intrepid backpackers.
GOVERNMENT RED TAPE ALSO TO BLAME

Investors said government red tape was partly responsible. Some said while government approval may be speedy at the central level, they can become tied up in negotiations with stubborn local officials or in ministerial bureaucracies.

Liao Khoon Ngain, an Ariston representative in Phnom Penh, blamed land disputes, noting his company has had to negotiate settlements with villagers who laid claim to properties in its development area.

Teng Huy said foreign investors would wait to see if Cambodia can become a stable democracy with steady land values. Until then, local investors are building nearly 40 small hotels with a total of 800 rooms.
Pech Arunn, a local businessman who has several small partnerships with foreign investors, including an uncanny replica of British pub in the southern port city, agreed.
"Everyone will wait until 1998," he said. "But I've already bought my property on the water. I can retire there and fish."
